_note: District matters are synthetic. Landmark matters are real Supreme Court cases from the original Supreme project, argued as they stood before judgment (old IPC/CrPC citations are correct for them).

cases.title: Anticipatory bail: State v. Ravi Kumar
cases.court: Court of the Additional Sessions Judge, Lucknow
cases.stage: Hearing on an application for anticipatory bail under Section 482, BNSS
cases.you_are: Counsel for the applicant, Ravi Kumar
facts: Ravi Kumar, 34, runs a small mobile repair shop in Aminabad.
A supplier, Sunil Traders, alleges Ravi took ₹2.4 lakh of phone parts on credit in March and never paid, and has filed an FIR for cheating under Section 318(4), BNS.
Ravi says he paid ₹1.6 lakh by UPI and that the remainder is a civil dispute over defective stock.
Ravi has no previous cases, has deep roots in Lucknow, and has offered to join the investigation.
The police have issued no notice under Section 35, BNSS so far; Ravi fears arrest.
bench_focus: Is this a civil dispute dressed as a criminal case?
UPI proof of ₹1.6 lakh
Flight risk and roots in the community
Will the applicant cooperate with the investigation?
Correct section: BNSS 482, not CrPC 438

cases.title: Cheque dishonour: Meenakshi Sundaram v. Karthik Raja
cases.court: Court of the Judicial Magistrate, Saidapet, Chennai
cases.stage: Hearing on the complaint under Section 138, Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
cases.you_are: Counsel for the complainant, Meenakshi Sundaram
facts: Meenakshi Sundaram lent ₹3,00,000 to her neighbour Karthik Raja in January for his daughter's college fees, by bank transfer.
Karthik gave a cheque for ₹3,00,000 dated 10 June. It was returned on 14 June with the memo 'Funds Insufficient'.
Meenakshi sent a demand notice by speed post on 2 July, received on 5 July.
No payment was made within 15 days. The complaint was filed on 8 August.
Karthik's defence: the cheque was a blank security cheque and the loan was ₹1,50,000, not ₹3,00,000.
bench_focus: Notice within 30 days of the return memo
Complaint within limitation
Legally enforceable debt and the bank transfer
Presumption under Section 139 NI Act
Blank security cheque defence

cases.title: Consumer complaint: Arjun Mehta v. ZipKart Electronics
cases.court: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Pune
cases.stage: Final arguments on a consumer complaint
cases.you_are: The complainant, appearing in person (Section 70, Consumer Protection Act, 2019)
facts: Arjun Mehta bought a ₹42,000 laptop from ZipKart Electronics' website in February.
The screen started flickering within three weeks. The service centre kept it twice for 18 days in total.
ZipKart refused a refund, saying the 7-day return window was over and only repair is covered.
Arjun has the invoice, three service job sheets and emails showing six complaints.
He seeks a refund, ₹25,000 compensation for harassment and ₹5,000 costs.
bench_focus: Deficiency in service vs manufacturing defect
Repeated repairs within warranty
Does the return window bar a refund for a defect?
How was ₹25,000 compensation calculated?
Proof of each complaint

cases.title: Ram Janmabhoomi v. Babri Masjid (2019)
cases.stage: Oral arguments before the Supreme Court, argued as the case stood before judgment
cases.summary: The historic land title dispute over the site in Ayodhya — balancing faith, history, and constitutional secularism.
facts: The historic land title dispute over the site in Ayodhya — balancing faith, history, and constitutional secularism.

M Siddiq (Sunni Waqf Board) (petitioner): Argued that the Babri Masjid stood on the disputed site since 1528, and the Muslim community held continuous title. Challenged the demolition as unconstitutional and demanded restoration of the mosque or full title rights to the land.

Mahant Suresh Das (Ram Lalla Virajman) (respondent): Argued that the disputed site is the birthplace of Lord Ram, that the deity holds juristic personality and inherent title to the land, and that faith and archaeological evidence support the Hindu claim to the site.
bench_focus: Can title be established by long possession alone?
What weight should the ASI excavation evidence carry?
Can a deity be a juristic person that holds land?
Does the Places of Worship Act, 1991 apply to this site?
What relief is just after the 1992 demolition?

petitioner.name: M Siddiq (Sunni Waqf Board)
key_args: The mosque stood for over 450 years — continuous possession establishes legal title under settled property law.
Demolition of the mosque in 1992 was an act of criminal destruction — the court cannot reward illegality.
Under Article 25-26, freedom of religion includes the right to maintain places of worship without interference.
Archaeological evidence is inconclusive and cannot override documented historical possession.
The Places of Worship Act, 1991 mandates maintaining the religious character of places as they existed on 15 August 1947.

respondent.name: Mahant Suresh Das (Ram Lalla Virajman)
respondent.position: Deity as Juristic Person — Claimant of Birthplace
key_args: Ram Lalla Virajman, the deity as a juristic person, has an inherent and inalienable right to the birthplace.
Archaeological Survey of India evidence confirms a pre-existing Hindu structure beneath the mosque.
The belief in Ram Janmasthan is ancient, unbroken, and constitutionally protected under Articles 25-26.
The doctrine of adverse possession cannot extinguish the rights of a deity — a deity never abandons its seat.
Hindu religious texts and traveller accounts across centuries confirm Ayodhya as the birthplace of Lord Ram.

cases.title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
cases.stage: Oral arguments before the Supreme Court, argued as the case stood before judgment
cases.summary: The foundational case that established the Basic Structure Doctrine — Parliament cannot amend the Constitution to destroy its essential features.
facts: The foundational case that established the Basic Structure Doctrine — Parliament cannot amend the Constitution to destroy its essential features.

Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru (petitioner): A religious leader from Kerala who challenged the 29th Amendment that placed the Kerala Land Reforms Act in the Ninth Schedule, arguing that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution is not unlimited and cannot destroy fundamental rights.

State of Kerala (respondent): Argued that Parliament, as the supreme representative body, has unlimited power to amend any provision of the Constitution under Article 368, including fundamental rights, to fulfill the directive principles of state policy.
bench_focus: Is there any implied limit on the power under Article 368?
What exactly forms the basic structure, and who decides it?
Should Golaknath be overruled?
Can the Ninth Schedule shut out judicial review?
How should Directive Principles be weighed against Part III?

petitioner.name: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru
key_args: Fundamental rights are not mere statutory provisions — they form the core identity of the Constitution.
Parliament derives its power FROM the Constitution; it cannot use that power to destroy the source itself.
The Ninth Schedule cannot be used as a shield to immunize legislation from fundamental rights review.
Article 368 grants power to amend, not to re-write or destroy the Constitution.
The framers intended fundamental rights to be inviolable — the Constituent Assembly debates confirm this.

respondent.name: State of Kerala
key_args: Article 368 confers plenary amendment power with no implied limitations — the text is clear.
Parliamentary sovereignty is the bedrock of democracy — elected representatives must have power to reshape law.
Land reforms are essential to fulfill Directive Principles under Part IV — fundamental rights cannot obstruct social justice.
The Golaknath decision was wrongly decided and must be overruled — it has no constitutional basis.
Judicial review of constitutional amendments itself undermines parliamentary supremacy and democratic governance.

cases.title: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
cases.stage: Oral arguments before the Supreme Court, argued as the case stood before judgment
cases.summary: The landmark ruling that decriminalized consensual homosexual acts by reading down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code.
facts: The landmark ruling that decriminalized consensual homosexual acts by reading down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code.

Navtej Singh Johar & Others (petitioner): A group of LGBTQ+ individuals including dancer Navtej Singh Johar challenged Section 377 as violating their fundamental rights to equality, non-discrimination, freedom of expression, and right to life and personal liberty.

Union of India (respondent): While the Union eventually left the matter to the Court's wisdom, the original defense argued that Section 377 reflected societal morality, that decriminalization should come through Parliament, and that the provision served public health interests.
bench_focus: Is consensual adult conduct in private protected by Article 21?
Does sex in Article 15 include sexual orientation?
Should the Court defer to Parliament on this?
Constitutional morality or public morality: which governs?
How do you deal with Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013)?

petitioner.name: Navtej Singh Johar & Others
key_args: Section 377 is a colonial relic from 1861 — it reflects Victorian morality, not Indian constitutional values.
Criminalizing consensual private conduct between adults violates the right to privacy under Article 21 (Puttaswamy).
Sexual orientation is an intrinsic part of identity — Article 15 prohibits discrimination on this ground.
The provision has a chilling effect on free expression and forces individuals to live in fear and secrecy.
The constitutional morality of inclusiveness must prevail over majoritarian social morality.

respondent.name: Union of India
key_args: Section 377 reflects the will of Parliament and prevailing societal moral standards.
Decriminalization of such conduct should come through legislative process, not judicial interpretation.
The provision serves legitimate state interests in public health and prevention of HIV/AIDS transmission.
Indian society's cultural and religious values do not endorse homosexual conduct.
The Suresh Kumar Koushal decision (2013) correctly upheld Section 377 — there's no reason to revisit it.

cases.title: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
cases.stage: Oral arguments before the Supreme Court, argued as the case stood before judgment
cases.summary: The nine-judge bench ruling that unanimously declared the Right to Privacy as a fundamental right under the Constitution.
facts: The nine-judge bench ruling that unanimously declared the Right to Privacy as a fundamental right under the Constitution.

Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) (petitioner): A retired High Court judge who challenged the Aadhaar scheme as violating citizens' right to privacy, arguing that privacy is an intrinsic part of life and personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution.

Union of India (respondent): Argued that there is no independent fundamental right to privacy, that previous Constitution Benches had settled this question, and that Aadhaar serves legitimate state interests in efficient welfare delivery and prevention of fraud.
bench_focus: Were M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh correctly decided?
Is privacy a standalone right or part of Article 21?
What test should limit privacy: legality, need, proportionality?
Does privacy cover personal data held by the State?
How should welfare delivery be balanced against privacy?

petitioner.name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.)
petitioner.position: Champion of the Right to Privacy
key_args: Privacy is not merely a statutory right — it is an intrinsic part of life and personal liberty under Article 21.
The M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh decisions wrongly denied privacy as a fundamental right and must be overruled.
Aadhaar creates a mass surveillance architecture that threatens individual autonomy and informational self-determination.
International human rights law recognizes privacy as a fundamental right — India cannot be an outlier.
The dignity of the individual, which is the cornerstone of Part III, necessarily includes the right to privacy.

respondent.name: Union of India
key_args: M.P. Sharma (8-judge bench) and Kharak Singh (6-judge bench) held that privacy is not a fundamental right.
Aadhaar serves compelling state interest — efficient delivery of subsidies and elimination of fraud worth crores.
An expansive right to privacy would impede legitimate state actions including law enforcement and national security.
Privacy, if recognized, must be subject to reasonable restrictions — it cannot be absolute.
The social welfare benefits of Aadhaar far outweigh any marginal privacy concerns.

cases.title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)
cases.stage: Oral arguments before the Supreme Court, argued as the case stood before judgment
cases.summary: The PIL that established binding guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace — laying the groundwork for gender justice in India.
facts: The PIL that established binding guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace — laying the groundwork for gender justice in India.

Vishaka & Other Women's Groups (petitioner): Women's rights organizations filed a PIL after the brutal gang-rape of Bhanwari Devi, a social worker in Rajasthan, demanding legal protection for women against sexual harassment at the workplace in the absence of legislation.

State of Rajasthan (respondent): The State argued that existing criminal law provisions were sufficient to deal with incidents of harassment and that legislative policy-making should be left to Parliament, not the judiciary.
bench_focus: Can the Court frame binding guidelines without a statute?
Can CEDAW be read into Article 21 when Parliament has not legislated?
Are the existing criminal provisions enough?
Who should be responsible: the employer or only the harasser?
Does this breach the separation of powers?

petitioner.name: Vishaka & Other Women's Groups
key_args: The gang-rape of Bhanwari Devi exposes a systemic failure — there is no law protecting working women from harassment.
Sexual harassment at the workplace violates Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g), and 21 of the Constitution.
In the absence of legislation, the Court must exercise its power under Article 32 to fill the legislative vacuum.
International conventions, especially CEDAW, obligate India to take measures against workplace harassment.
The right to work with dignity is a fundamental right — it cannot exist without freedom from sexual harassment.

respondent.name: State of Rajasthan
key_args: Existing provisions under the IPC (Sections 354, 509) adequately address acts of sexual harassment.
Framing guidelines with the force of law is a legislative function — the Court would be overstepping its role.
Individual incidents, however tragic, should not lead to judicial law-making that bypasses Parliament.
The separation of powers doctrine requires deference to the legislature on policy matters.
Administrative mechanisms within organizations are better suited than blanket judicial mandates.
